transcript: There is a lot of New York theatre that's closing in June that you're running out of time to see. So here is an incomplete, but still surprisingly large roundup of shows closing before the end of June in in order of soonest closing date to latest. Unfortunately I'm posting this a little too late for the June 7th shows. I'm posting this on June 5th, but I'll just give a shout out to Fallen Angels on Broadway. Indian Princesses at Atlantic, about a group of young girls of color with white fathers. And the premiere production of a lost play from Thorton Wilder, The Emporium, which I posted about recently. The other night I saw Derangements at Clubbed Thumb. This is by one of the co-writers of the musical Hole! and it was very much my sense of humor. I thought it was one of the funniest shows I've seen all year. It starts with two friends having lunch, but something strange happens to them and it triggers this bizarre series of events. We have the revival of Becky Shaw, which is a very dark, acerbic comedy. It took a while for it to grow on me, but by the end I loved it. This one has a very starry cast, but Alden Ehrenreich is kind of the performance everyone's talking about. Animal wisdom is the show by Heather Christian that gave me a panic attack in the theater, which I talked about in a previous video, but as I said in that video, I would still recommend it if you think it it’s up your alley the Maid I'm seeing tonight. This is a reimagining of the Jean Genet play by the same director who did the Dorian Gray with Sarah Snook and the Dracula with Cynthia Erivo. Then, of course, we have Mexodus. This one of the most buzzed-about new musicals of the season. This one's definitely worth checking out. For one week only, the international tour of Sting’s The Last Ship It is coming to New York, and Sting himself is starring in it. I was a big fan of this show when I saw it on Broadway, and I'm curious to see the revisions. Also one of the most buzzed about plays with some of the best actors in New York is the return engagement of well, I'll let you go. Girls Chance Music by Eisa Davis, about a group of girls in a music program in Berkeley. Then we have Jerome, about an older, gay throuple in 1992 Arizona. I found it really absorbing and emotionally engaging with a lot of cool stagecraft, although I can tell that this play has not been for everybody. Speaking of not for everybody, just throwing out there that the revival of chess is also closing in June. You have the Balusters, which seems to be for everybody except for me. I wasn't a big fan of this play, but everyone else seems to love it. Tempest Tossed is an abridged and partly adapted version of the Tempest, performed in this very cool old house. And of course we have KenRex, which is a pretty acclaimed one person show transferring from London. He makes great use of physicality to play all these characters, combined with very cool lighting and sound and live music to bring this true crime story to life. We have the return engagement of Can I Be Frank, a solo show from Morgan Bassichis, directed by Sam Pinkleton. It's sort of about the legacy of queer comedians by looking back on the comedian Frank Maya. Another return engagement, A woman among women, which is inspired by Arthur Miller's all my sons. And it's done really beautifully in this tender way. Of course we have the public theatre’s Shakespeare in the park production of Romeo and Juliet and their mobile unit production of as you like it. Then we have three more Broadway shows closing, including, of course, Death Becomes her, unfortunately ending its run, but then also the limited run of Giant is ending, starring John Lithgow as Roald Dahl and the play adaptation of the film Dog Day Afternoon, starring Jon Bernthall and Ebon Moss-Bachrach from the Bear. But we're still not done. I have two more for you. We have the circuit, which is, as you can see, an immersive silent disco ballet performed in Dumbo. I'm seeing this this weekend. I'm very curious. And ending with the third and final show, In Clubbed Thumb’s beloved summerworks series The Family Dog, in which “Whitney returns to her childhood home to say goodbye to the pet who replaced her. Miracles abound, some in meatball form.”
